= Getting Started with TypeScript
:description: Install TypeScript, compile a first file, and understand that types are checked then erased -- code generation is independent of type-checking and errors do not block emit by default.
:keywords: TypeScript, tsc, install TypeScript, erasable types, type stripping, ts-node, tsx, Deno, Bun, TypeScript Playground, compile pipeline, noEmitOnError
:page-aliases: web/typescript/getting-started.adoc

include::partial$ai-disclaimer.adoc[]

TypeScript is JavaScript with a static type layer that the compiler checks and then throws away. You write
`.ts`, `tsc` verifies the types and emits ordinary `.js` -- nothing about the running program changes. If you
have five minutes, read https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/typescript-in-5-minutes.html[TypeScript
in 5 minutes] first; this page is the hands-on version.

== An erasable typed superset of JavaScript

Every valid JavaScript file is already a valid TypeScript file. TypeScript only *adds* annotations, and those
annotations exist only at compile time: they are checked, then stripped. There are no runtime types, no
reflection, and no runtime cost.

[source,ts]
----
function greet(user: { name: string; age: number }): string {
  return `Hello, ${user.name} (${user.age})`;
}

const alice = { name: "Alice", age: 30 };
console.log(greet(alice));
----

Compiled with `tsc` (targeting a modern runtime), the emitted JavaScript is what you would have written by
hand -- the shape at runtime is identical:

[source,js]
----
function greet(user) {
    return `Hello, ${user.name} (${user.age})`;
}
const alice = { name: "Alice", age: 30 };
console.log(greet(alice));
----

Type-checking and code generation are *independent passes*. By default a type error is reported but does
**not** stop the emit:

[source,ts]
----
let count: number = 1;
count = "two";
----

[source,console]
----
$ npx tsc bad.ts
bad.ts:2:1 - error TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.

2 count = "two";
  ~~~~~

Found 1 error in bad.ts:2
----

`bad.js` is still written, containing `count = "two"`. Set `noEmitOnError` in `tsconfig.json` (or pass
`--noEmitOnError`) when you want a failed check to suppress output -- the usual choice for CI. See
xref:programming-languages/typescript/tsconfig-and-compiler-options.adoc[tsconfig and Compiler Options] for the switches that
shape the emit.

== Install and first compile

Install TypeScript as a per-project dev dependency so every checkout builds against a known version:

[source,bash]
----
npm i -D typescript          # local dev dependency
npx tsc --version

npx tsc --init               # writes tsconfig.json with strict defaults
npx tsc                      # compile every file the tsconfig includes
npx tsc --watch              # recompile on save (alias: -w)
npx tsc hello.ts             # one-off: compile a single file, ignoring tsconfig
----

The https://www.typescriptlang.org/download/[download page] covers global installs, other package managers,
and the nightly build.

Create `hello.ts`:

[source,ts]
----
const who: string = process.argv[2] ?? "world";
console.log(`Hello, ${who}!`);
----

Compile it and run the output with Node:

[source,bash]
----
npx tsc hello.ts        # produces hello.js
node hello.js TypeScript
# -> Hello, TypeScript!
----

=== Running .ts directly with type-stripping runners

Several tools run a `.ts` file without a separate build step by erasing the types in memory:

[source,bash]
----
npx tsx hello.ts                          # tsx
npx ts-node hello.ts                      # ts-node
node --experimental-strip-types hello.ts  # Node (built-in; unflagged in current releases)
deno run hello.ts                         # Deno -- TS support is native
bun hello.ts                              # Bun -- TS support is native
----

Caveat: these **run but do not type-check**. The `count = "two"` program above executes to completion under
every one of them. Keep `npx tsc --noEmit`, your editor, or a CI step as the real type gate. Node's built-in
stripping is the strictest -- it rejects TypeScript syntax that emits code (`enum`, `namespace`, parameter
properties), so it only accepts genuinely erasable syntax.

For Node's type stripping in depth, see xref:backend/nodejs/typescript-in-nodejs.adoc[TypeScript in Node.js].

== The Playground and your editor

The https://www.typescriptlang.org/play/[TypeScript Playground] is the compiler running in your browser:
paste TypeScript and see the emitted JavaScript, the errors, the generated `.d.ts`, and every compiler
option as a toggle. Each session is a shareable URL, which is why most examples in the official docs link
straight into it.

Locally, VS Code bundles the TypeScript language service, so hover, go-to-definition, autocomplete, rename,
and inline errors work in `.ts` (and `.js`) files with no extension to install; other editors reach the same
service over the Language Server Protocol (see xref:programming-languages/typescript/ides-and-tools.adoc[TypeScript IDEs & Tools]
for the common choices). Use your editor to *interrogate the type system* -- hover a value
to see what TypeScript inferred, rather than guessing:

[source,ts]
----
const ids = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n.toString());
//    ^? const ids: string[]
// Hover `ids` in the editor, or use the `//   ^?` twoslash query in the Playground.
----

== What TypeScript is not

* *Not a runtime.* There is no "TypeScript engine". The output is plain JavaScript for Node, Deno, Bun, or a
  browser. `tsc` itself is TypeScript compiled to JavaScript.
* *Not a linter.* It checks types, not style or best practices. Run ESLint alongside it for rules like
  "unused variables are an error" or "prefer const declarations".
* *Not a rewrite of your logic.* Erasing the annotations from a `.ts` file gives back working `.js`. The few
  constructs that do emit extra code (`enum`, `namespace`, constructor parameter properties, legacy
  `experimentalDecorators`) are opt-in and avoidable.
* *Not slower JavaScript.* Types cost compile time only. The shipped code carries zero type-related
  overhead -- nothing is added, checked, or reflected at runtime.

== The compile pipeline

[mermaid]
....
flowchart LR
    A[".ts source"] --> B["parse<br/>(build AST)"]
    B --> C["bind<br/>(symbols and scopes)"]
    C --> D["type-check<br/>(report errors)"]
    D --> E["transform<br/>(strip types, downlevel syntax)"]
    E --> F["emit"]
    F --> G[".js"]
    F --> H[".d.ts&nbsp;&mdash; with declaration"]
    F --> I[".js.map&nbsp;&mdash; with sourceMap"]
    D -. "errors are reported but do NOT stop emit<br/>unless noEmitOnError is set" .-> E
....

The `type-check` and `transform` stages share the parsed AST but are otherwise decoupled: by default `tsc`
prints every error and *still* writes the `.js`. `noEmitOnError` is what ties a clean type-check to a
successful build. Declaration files (`.d.ts`) and source maps (`.js.map`) are produced by the same emit step
when `declaration` and `sourceMap` are enabled.

== A first project, end to end

A single file is enough to see the idea, but a real project has a `tsconfig.json`, a source folder and an output
folder. This walk-through builds the smallest version of that shape using the request-state type that the
xref:programming-languages/typescript/worked-example.adoc[worked example] develops. The layout is:

[source,text]
----
proj/
  package.json        { "type": "module" }
  tsconfig.json
  src/
    state.ts          the RequestState union and describe()
    main.ts           uses it
  dist/               created by tsc
----

Create `tsconfig.json`. `tsc --init` writes a config with many options commented out and a handful switched
on (`strict`, `module: nodenext`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `skipLibCheck` and others); the version below keeps
only what this project needs, plus `noEmitOnError` so a failed check never produces output:

[source,json]
----
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "rootDir": "src",
    "outDir": "dist",
    "sourceMap": true,
    "declaration": true,
    "noEmitOnError": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}
----

`src/state.ts`:

[source,typescript]
----
export type RequestState<T> =
  | { readonly kind: "idle" }
  | { readonly kind: "loading" }
  | { readonly kind: "success"; readonly data: T }
  | { readonly kind: "error"; readonly error: string };

export function describe<T>(state: RequestState<T>): string {
  switch (state.kind) {
    case "idle":
      return "nothing yet";
    case "loading":
      return "loading...";
    case "success":
      return "got " + JSON.stringify(state.data);
    case "error":
      return "failed: " + state.error;
  }
}
----

`src/main.ts`:

[source,typescript]
----
import { describe, type RequestState } from "./state.js";

const states: RequestState<{ name: string }>[] = [
  { kind: "idle" },
  { kind: "loading" },
  { kind: "success", data: { name: "Ada" } },
  { kind: "error", error: "HTTP 500" },
];

for (const s of states) {
  console.log(describe(s));
}
----

Build and run it. The import specifier says `./state.js` even though the file on disk is `state.ts`: TypeScript
checks the specifier as it will exist *after* compilation, which is what Node will load. `--listEmittedFiles`
shows exactly what the compiler wrote:

[source,console]
----
$ npx tsc -p . --listEmittedFiles
TSFILE: .../dist/state.js
TSFILE: .../dist/state.js.map
TSFILE: .../dist/state.d.ts
TSFILE: .../dist/main.js
TSFILE: .../dist/main.js.map
TSFILE: .../dist/main.d.ts

$ node dist/main.js
nothing yet
loading...
got {"name":"Ada"}
failed: HTTP 500
----

== What the compiler produced

Three files come out for each input, each with a different audience. `dist/state.js` is what runs: the type alias
and every annotation are gone, and nothing else changed.

[source,js]
----
export function describe(state) {
    switch (state.kind) {
        case "idle":
            return "nothing yet";
        case "loading":
            return "loading...";
        case "success":
            return "got " + JSON.stringify(state.data);
        case "error":
            return "failed: " + state.error;
    }
}
//# sourceMappingURL=state.js.map
----

`dist/state.d.ts` is what *other TypeScript projects* read when they import this module. It keeps only the type
information, with no function bodies:

[source,typescript]
----
export type RequestState<T> = {
    readonly kind: "idle";
} | {
    readonly kind: "loading";
} | {
    readonly kind: "success";
    readonly data: T;
} | {
    readonly kind: "error";
    readonly error: string;
};
export declare function describe<T>(state: RequestState<T>): string;
----

`state.js.map` is a source map, which lets a debugger or a stack trace point back at `state.ts`. Notice also that
`dist/main.js` begins `+import { describe } from "./state.js";+`: the `type RequestState` specifier was erased
because it names only a type.

[mermaid]
....
flowchart LR
    S1["src/state.ts"] --> TC["tsc: parse, bind, check"]
    S2["src/main.ts"] --> TC
    CFG["tsconfig.json"] --> TC
    TC -->|"errors?"| G{"noEmitOnError<br/>and errors?"}
    G -->|"no"| J["dist/*.js"]
    G -->|"no"| D["dist/*.d.ts"]
    G -->|"no"| M["dist/*.js.map"]
    G -->|"yes"| X["nothing written,<br/>exit code 1"]
    J --> N["node dist/main.js"]
....

== A failed check, with and without `noEmitOnError`

Change one return value so it has the wrong type, `return 42;` in the `loading` case, and run the build again.
The checker rejects it, and because `noEmitOnError` is set, `dist` is not created:

[source,console]
----
$ npx tsc -p .
src/state.ts(12,7): error TS2322: Type 'number' is not assignable to type 'string'.
$ echo $?
1
$ ls dist
ls: dist: No such file or directory
----

Remove `noEmitOnError` and the same error is still reported, the exit code is still non-zero, but the JavaScript
is written anyway. That is the behaviour of a bare `tsc file.ts` and of the type-stripping runners: types are one
pass, code generation is another. The exit code is what a CI job should look at.

== Type stripping in Node, in practice

Recent Node releases can execute `.ts` files directly by erasing annotations in memory. Two behaviours are worth
seeing once, so they do not surprise you later. The first is that nothing is checked: a program with a type error
runs normally.

[source,console]
----
$ cat bad.ts
let count: number = 1;
count = "two";
console.log(count);
$ node bad.ts
two
----

The second is that only *erasable* syntax is accepted. `enum` needs generated code, so the stripper refuses it:

[source,console]
----
$ cat en.ts
enum Color { Red, Green }
console.log(Color.Green);
$ node en.ts
SyntaxError [ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX]: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode
----

Pair stripping with `"erasableSyntaxOnly": true` in `tsconfig.json` so that your editor flags such syntax before
Node does, and keep `tsc --noEmit` as the type gate.

== Two beginner pitfalls

* *Host APIs need their types.* `console` comes from the default `lib` (which includes the DOM typings), but
  `process`, `Buffer` and Node's modules come from `@types/node`. `tsc --init` writes `"types": []`, so after
  `npm i -D @types/node` you must also list it (`"types": ["node"]`) or the compiler will report that it cannot
  find the name `process`. See xref:backend/nodejs/typescript-in-nodejs.adoc[TypeScript in Node.js].
* *Defaults differ between compiler versions.* A bare `tsc hello.ts` with no config and no `--target` emits
  ES5-level JavaScript (`let` becomes `var`) under TypeScript 5.9, while the 7.0 compiler emits modern syntax with
  a `"use strict"` prologue. Do not depend on defaults: set `target`, `module` and `strict` explicitly, as in the
  config above.
